passage: Saturday. Six months since I started meeting Sangeeta, so today's session was a review. We went through the list from January. Done: portfolio site, two mock interviews, and a first proper offer letter. Not done: the open-source contribution. Sangeeta said she still wants it, so it stays, but on her own with a check-in from me. Then I raised the thing I'd been putting off: maybe we don't need regular sessions anymore. I worried it would sound like I was pulling away. Sangeeta grinned and said she'd been thinking the same and would rather message me when stuck. So we're moving to one catch-up every two months, plus messages anytime. Strange, but it feels like a finish line, not a door closing. — Naveen

Pallavi: six months today! want to do our review?
Ayesha: yes. I made a list 😅
Ayesha: goals from march: 1. get promoted to analyst II, done 2. present at a team meeting, done (twice!) 3. learn SQL properly, half done
Pallavi: that's a strong six months. what's left?
Ayesha: just SQL. I have a course for it
Pallavi: so here's my honest thought. you don't need fortnightly calls anymore. how about we move to a check-in every two months?
Ayesha: is that... you getting rid of me?
Pallavi: the opposite. it means you did it. regular sessions were for getting you here
Ayesha: ok. that actually feels good when you put it like that
Pallavi: and you can always message if something big comes up. that doesn't end

passage:
Six months after they first met at the tea stall outside the Anand bus depot, Chinmay and Charu sat in the same spot with the same notebook. Charu had started a small milk delivery service for thirty homes; Chinmay, who had run one before, had been meeting her every other Saturday.
'Let's look at what you wanted in January,' Chinmay said, opening the first page. 'A route that runs without you on the scooter every day. Done, you have two delivery boys. Books that balance each month. Done. Fifty homes by June.' 'Forty-two,' Charu said. 'Close enough to handle myself.'
Chinmay closed the notebook. 'Then I think we stop the Saturdays. Not because I'm leaving. Because you don't need them.' Charu looked unsure, then smiled. 'Call you if the cows go on strike?' 'Any time.'

qa.q: How many homes does Charu deliver to now?
What might Charu have been feeling when she looked unsure?
qa.a: Charu may have felt a moment of worry at losing the regular support, then pride in no longer needing it.

qa.q: What else could Chinmay do to keep the door open?
qa.a: Chinmay could suggest a check-in in a few months, and make clear that Charu can call when something big comes up.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel closing the notebook?
qa.a: Chinmay likely feels satisfied, seeing the end of the Saturdays as proof the mentoring worked.

grounding: It shows a mentor and mentee reviewing goals after six months and moving to occasional contact, treating the end of regular meetings as success.
